newsitem.title: INDIA: India commodity prices rise on truck strike.
newsitem.headline: India commodity prices rise on truck strike.

text.p: Indian commodity prices crept up in the domestic market as a strike by truck operators brought the movement of goods to an abrupt halt, industry officials and traders said on Friday.
"The strike has stalled new crop arrivals," Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, told Reuters.
"Prices of edible oil have moved up but not to a very great extent as there are reasonable stocks of imported oil. But the impact would be much more if the strike continues beyond Monday."

Truck owners launched an indefinite strike on Tuesday in protest against a five percent service tax on road transport which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed in the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March).
The protest has kept some 2.2 million trucks off the roads and crippled the movement of goods and services.
Industry officials said prices of edible oil had risen as the summer oilseed crop arrivals had come to a standstill.
Traders said groundnut oil prices had risen to 35,500 rupees ($991) per tonne from 34,700 rupees and palm olein oil prices had gone up to 28,500 rupees from 28,000 last week.

P.C. Mutha, deputy chairman of the Soybean Processors Association of India said: "The arrivals have become negligible in the Central Indian markets. No soybean is reaching the factories and therefore (there is) no refining."
Mutha said soybean oil prices had risen to 28,000 rupees per tonne from 27,000 rupees in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, which contributes 80 percent of the country's soybean production.

"The strike has affected prices as local demand (for rice) is there but cargoes are not moving," Prem Garg, managing director, of Sri Lal Mahal Overseas, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter, told Reuters.
Garg said rice prices in the local markets had risen by 500 rupees per tonne during the last four days. "This has somewhat reflected in the export prices also."

"Sugar prices have gone up in some consuming centres," S.L. Jain, Indian Sugar Mills Association, told Reuters. "The strike has affected the sugar industry as traders were not able to lift stocks from millers."
Jain said jute bags were not able to reach the factories in time for packing due to the strike.
"Prices are going up in the terminal markets due to non-availability and are falling in producing centres due to a glut," a Bombay based commodity analyst, told Reuters.
He said the state-run grain procurement agency the Food Corporation of India had been unable to buy wheat from farmers in the absence of proper transport.
